source.notes: Paper prints Series LKM4N, 'SET~1' (stored as SET-1), Q.P. Code 32/4/1, 32 printed pages (including 1 map), 38 questions, Maximum Marks 80, Time allowed 3 hours. Session is not printed. English text is on odd pages (Hindi on even pages). Q.P. codes 32/1/1, 32/1/2, 32/1/3, 32/2/1, 32/2/2, 32/2/3, 32/3/1, 32/3/2 and 32/3/3 in the same archive are scanned image PDFs with almost no usable text layer (pdftotext returns under 30 characters each) and were skipped; 32/4/1 is the first Q.P. code (by printed code order) with a usable text layer and a matching marking-scheme section (087_32_4_1_E.pdf). Two 'visually impaired' alternative questions (in lieu of Q.3 and Q.21) are not imported as separate entries, since they duplicate the question number without a distinct printed sub-part label. For Q.9 (map question), sub-part B ('the place where the session of the Indian National Congress was held') is not imported: unlike sub-part A, its printed clue alone does not uniquely identify one place without the marked point on the map (the marking scheme's only textual confirmation, 'Calcutta (Kolkata)', comes from the more specific Visually-Impaired alternative clue 'held in 1920 in Eastern India', which is not printed for the main question). Q.13's fill-in-the-blank statement text is missing from the PDF text layer in both English and Hindi (only the instruction line, mark value and options extracted); confidence is set LOW for that item. Q.19 (map-based, Geography) prints four 1-mark items of which candidates attempt any three (worth 3 marks); all four are imported since each stands alone, so the sum of printed marks for Q.19 (4) exceeds the 3 actually achievable.

questions.text: “Food offered many examples of long distance cultural exchange during pre-modern times.” Explain the statement with any two examples.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) Common food such as potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies, sweet potatoes etc. are believed to be introduced in Europe and Asia from America.
(ii) Spaghetti and noodles travelled west from China.
(iii) Any other relevant point.
(Any two points to be explained.)

questions.text: “Trade and cultural exchange went hand-in-hand during pre-modern times.” Explain the statement with any two examples.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) The silk routes are example of pre-modern trade and cultural links between distant parts of the world.
(ii) Chinese silk, pottery and textiles from India and Southeast Asia travelled to Europe and precious metals flowed from Europe to Asia.
(iii) Early Christian missionaries and Muslim preachers travelled this route to Asia.
(iv) Buddhism emerged from eastern India and spread in several directions through intersecting points on the silk routes.
(v) Any other relevant point.
(Any two points to be explained.)

questions.text: Evaluate the role of Buddhist Missionaries in printing culture.

officialAnswer.text:

(ii) The oldest Japanese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.
(iii) Pictures were printed on textiles, playing cards and paper money.
(iv) Any other relevant point.

questions.text: Describe the process of unification of Germany.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) Nationalist feelings were widespread among middle-class Germans, who in 1848 tried to unite the different regions of the German confederation into a nation-state governed by an elected parliament.
(ii) This liberal initiative to nation-building was repressed by the combined forces of the monarchy and the military, supported by the large landowners (called Junkers) of Prussia.
(iii) Prussia took on the leadership of the movement for national unification.
(iv) Its chief minister, Otto von Bismarck, was the architect of this process carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy.
(v) Three wars over seven years – with Austria, Denmark and France – ended in Prussian victory and completed the process of unification.
(Any five points to be described.)

questions.text: Describe the process of unification of Italy.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) During the middle of the nineteenth century, Italy was divided into seven states, of which only one, Sardinia-Piedmont, was ruled by an Italian princely house.
(ii) The north was under Austrian Habsburgs, the centre was ruled by the Pope and the southern regions were under the domination of the Bourbon kings of Spain.
(iii) During the 1830s, Giuseppe Mazzini had sought to put together a coherent programme for a unitary Italian Republic.
(iv) The failure of revolutionary uprisings both in 1831 and 1848 meant that the mantle now fell on Sardinia-Piedmont under its ruler King Victor Emmanuel II to unify the Italian states through war.
(v) In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy.
(Any five points to be described.)…

questions.text:
Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow :
Quit India Movement
The failure of the Cripps Mission and the effects of World War II created widespread discontentment in India. This led Gandhiji to launch a movement calling for complete withdrawal of the British from India. The Congress Working Committee, in its meeting in Wardha on 14 July 1942, passed the historic ‘Quit India’ resolution demanding the immediate transfer of power to Indians and quit India. On 8th August 1942 in Bombay, the All India Congress Committee endorsed the resolution which called for a non-violent mass struggle on the widest possible scale throughout the country. It was on this occasion that Gandhiji delivered the famous ‘Do or Die’ speech. The call for ‘Quit India’ almost brought the state machinery to a standstill in large parts of the country as people voluntarily threw themselves into the thick of the movement. People observed hartals, and demonstrations and processions were accompanied by national songs and slogans. The movement was truly a mass movement which brought into its ambit thousands of ordinary people, namely students, workers and peasants. It also saw the active participation of leaders, namely, Jayprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali and Ram Manohar Lohia and many women such as Matangini Hazra in Bengal, Kanaklata Barua in Assam and Rama Devi in Orissa. The British responded with much force, yet it took more than a year to suppress the movement.
8.1 How did the failure of the Cripps Mission contribute to the launch of the Quit India Movement ? (1)
8.2 Why was Gandhiji’s call for ‘the Quit India’ considered historic ? (1)
8.3 Explain the role of women in making the Quit India Movement more inclusive. (2)
extractionIssues: Sub-questions 8.1–8.3 are printed on page 11 (facing English page), continuing this passage from page 9
Sub-part marks shown in brackets were printed in the margin

officialAnswer.text:
(8.1) The failure of the Cripps Mission created widespread discontentment in India. This led Gandhiji to launch Quit India movement calling for complete withdrawal of the British from India. (Any one point)
(8.2) The Congress Working Committee, in its meeting in Wardha on 14 July 1942, passed the historic ‘Quit India’ resolution demanding the immediate transfer of power to Indians and quit India. (Any one point)
(8.3) The Quit India movement saw the active participation of many women leaders like Aruna Asaf Ali and Matangini Hazra in Bengal, Kanaklata Barua in Assam and Rama Devi in Orissa; they participated in large numbers in hartals, demonstrations and processions accompanied by national songs and slogans. (Any two points)

questions.text:
Read the given source and answer the questions that follow :
Sardar Sarovar Project
Sardar Sarovar Dam has been built over the Narmada river in Gujarat. This is one of the largest water resources projects of India covering four states – Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Rajasthan. The Sardar Sarovar Project would meet the requirement of water in drought prone and desert areas. Sardar Sarovar Project will provide irrigation facilities to 18.45 lakh hectare of land, covering 3112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. It will also irrigate 2,46,000 hectare of land in the strategic desert districts of Barmer and Jalore in Rajasthan and 37,500 hectare in the tribal hilly tract of Maharashtra through lift. About 75% of the command area in Gujarat is drought prone while entire command in Rajasthan is drought prone. Assured water supply will soon make this area drought proof.
18.1 Why is Sardar Sarovar Project considered important for Gujarat ? (1)
18.2 Why is Sardar Sarovar Project designed to cover four states ? (1)
18.3 In what ways does this project promote sustainability ? (2)

officialAnswer.text:
(18.1) Sardar Sarovar Project provides irrigation facilities to 18.45 lakh hectare of land, covering 3112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. (Any one point)
(18.2) The project is designed to cover the requirement of water in drought prone and desert areas of all four states, and to provide irrigation facilities in some areas of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. (Any one point)
(18.3) (i) Provides drinking water to drought prone areas. (ii) Irrigates large areas of agricultural land, ensuring food security. (iii) Generates hydro-electric energy, a renewable and clean source. (iv) Ensures recharge of ground water, supporting sustainable water management. (Any two points)

questions.text: Differentiate between democracy and dictatorship.
extractionIssues: Official answer is a two-column table (Democracy / Dictatorship); flattened row by row

officialAnswer.text:
Democracy | Dictatorship
(i) A form of government where people elect their leaders. | A form of government where people have no role in selecting the ruler.
(ii) Government is accountable to the citizens. | Government is not accountable to the citizens.
(iii) Power lies with the people. | Power lies with one person or a small group of people.
(iv) Free & fair elections are held at regular intervals. | Either elections are not held or they are not free and fair.
(v) People enjoy rights and freedom. | People do not get rights and freedom.
(Any two points of difference to be explained.)

questions.text: How does the Indian Constitution define the distribution of powers between the centre and the states ? Explain with examples.

officialAnswer.text: The Constitution provides a three-fold distribution of legislative powers between the Union Government and the State Governments, containing three lists: (i) Union List includes subjects of national importance such as defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency; the Union Government alone makes laws on these. (ii) State List contains subjects of state and local importance such as police, trade, education, forest; the State Government makes laws on these. (iii) Concurrent List includes subjects of common interest to both, such as education and forest; both can legislate, and Union law prevails in case of conflict. (Any three points to be explained.)

questions.text: Examine the role of political parties in a democracy.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) Parties contest elections; in most democracies, elections are fought mainly among candidates put up by political parties.
(ii) Parties put forward different policies and programmes and the voters choose from them.
(iii) Parties play a decisive role in making laws for a country.
(iv) Parties form and run governments; big policy decisions are taken by political executives from the political parties.
(v) Parties losing elections play the role of opposition, voicing different views and criticising government for its failures.
(Any five points to be examined.)

questions.text: Examine the need of the political parties in a democratic government.

officialAnswer.text:
(i) In large and complex societies, political parties are needed to gather different views on various issues to present them to government.
(ii) Political parties are needed to bring together representatives to form a responsible government.
(iii) In the absence of political parties every candidate in the elections will be independent, so no one will be able to make any promise about a major policy change.
(iv) Political parties are needed to support or restrain the government.
(v) Political parties are crucial in making policies, justifying them or opposing them.
(Any five points to be examined.)

questions.text:
Read the given source carefully and answer the questions that follow :
Power Sharing
Power is shared among different organs of government, such as the legislature, executive and judiciary. Let us call this horizontal distribution of power because it allows different organs of government placed at the same level to exercise different powers. Such a separation ensures that none of the organs can exercise unlimited power. Each organ checks the others. This results in a balance of power among various institutions. Last year, we studied that in a democracy, even though ministers and government officials exercise power, they are responsible to the Parliament or State Assemblies. Similarly, although judges are appointed by the executive, they can check the functioning of executive or laws made by the legislatures. This arrangement is called a system of checks and balances.
28.1 Explain the term ‘Balance of Power’. (1)
28.2 Why is the judiciary considered independent in a democracy ? (1)
28.3 How is power shared among different organs of government ? (2)

officialAnswer.text:
(28.1) None of the organs can exercise unlimited power; each organ checks the others. (Any one point)
(28.2) Judges are appointed by the executive, but they can check the functioning of the executive or laws made by the legislatures. (Any one point)
(28.3) There are three organs of government – Legislative, Executive and Judiciary – placed at the same level to exercise different powers. Legislature formulates law, executive implements it, and judiciary interprets the laws and resolves disputes. (Any two points)

questions.text: How are primary sectors different from secondary sectors ? Explain with examples.
extractionIssues: Official answer is a two-column table (Primary Sector / Secondary Sector); flattened row by row

officialAnswer.text:
Primary Sector | Secondary Sector
(i) Goods are produced by exploiting natural resources. | Natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing.
(ii) It produces raw materials. | It uses the produce of the primary sector to change it into manufactured goods.
(iii) Products are from agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry. | Manufacturing is done in a workshop or factory.
(iv) Also called agriculture and related sector; forms the basis of rural economy. | Also called Industrial sector; forms the basis of urban economy.
(v) Example – farming, fishing, mining. | Example – cotton to cloth, sugarcane to sugar.
(Any five points of difference to be explained.)

questions.text: How are organized sectors different from unorganized sectors ? Explain with examples.
extractionIssues: Official answer is a two-column table (Organised Sector / Unorganised Sector) whose column order was scrambled by the PDF extractor; rows below were reconstructed by pairing the extracted phrases (same wording, reordered) — check against the PDF

officialAnswer.text:
Organised Sector | Unorganised Sector
(i) The terms of employment are regular. | The terms of employment are not regular.
(ii) It is governed by government rules and regulations such as Factory Act, Minimum Wage Act etc. | It is largely outside the control of the government; there are rules and regulations but these are not followed.
(iii) Workers in the organised sector enjoy security of employment. | Workers in the unorganised sector do not have security of employment.
(iv) They get paid leave; there is provision of provident fund, gratuity etc. | They do not get paid leave; there is no provision of provident fund, gratuity etc.
(v) Example – Railway, post office etc. | Example – Street vendors, domestic help, agricultural labourers etc.
(Any five points to be explained with example.)
